builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: HiCal: Offline Calibration for Hierarchical Scale Encoding in Accurate HiF4 Quantization
summary: It replaces the fixed rounding rule and scale-extension thresholds of standard HiF4 block floating-point quantization with offline-calibrated rounding bias and empirically optimized Level-2/Level-3 thresholds, keeping the deterministic per-block encoding unchanged at inference. It costs only a one-time offline calibration on representative tensor statistics, with no added inference latency, no per-block candidate search, and no extra memory; the residual cost is implementation effort in the quantization pipeline. It can fail if the deployment target lacks HiF4 hardware or kernel support, if calibration data distributions drift from production activations, and the reported end-to-end gains (about one percentage point) may be too small to survive integration overhead.
rationale: HiCal is an offline, inference-cost-free calibration of HiF4 scale encoding, so it is worth adopting if the deployment stack uses HiF4, but its relevance is conditional on that specific hardware format and its end-to-end gains are modest.
technique: Offline calibration of HiF4 hierarchical scale encoding

claims.statement: It replaces the fixed rounding rule and scale-extension thresholds of standard HiF4 block floating-point quantization with offline-calibrated rounding bias and empirically optimized Level-2/Level-3 thresholds, keeping the deterministic per-block encoding unchanged at inference. It costs only a one-time offline calibration on representative tensor statistics, with no added inference latency, no per-block candidate search, and no extra memory; the residual cost is implementation effort in the quantization pipeline. It can fail if the deployment target lacks HiF4 hardware or kernel support, if calibration data distributions drift from production activations, and the reported end-to-end gains (about one percentage point) may be too small to survive integration overhead.
Reduces quantization MSE by 9.91%-23.50% versus original HiF4 (13.00% on real Qwen3-8B activations) and improves average benchmark scores by 0.91 points on Qwen3-8B and 1.25 points on Qwen3-30B-A3B.
